questions.mindset: Agree how decisions will be made before the first one arrives.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme replacing a national charity's donor database, the governance plan sets your approval limit at £10,000 and the sponsor's at £100,000, and says any wider delegation must be recorded in a delegation schedule approved by the board. You need a decision on extending the data-migration supplier's contract by three months at £45,000. When you send the sponsor your analysis, she replies: 'You know this better than I do. Just decide, I trust you.' What should you do?

options.text: Make the decision on the strength of her email, which gives you written authority from the sponsor, and record it in the decision log.
options.rationale: An unlimited 'just decide' is not a delegation the governance plan recognises, since it requires a recorded entry in the board-approved schedule. The candidate treats goodwill in writing as authority in writing.

options.text: Raise with the board chair that the sponsor is not fulfilling her role as decision-maker, so that the extension can be considered and approved by the full board instead.
options.rationale: The sponsor has expressed confidence, not neglect, and going over her head damages a working relationship to solve a problem a short note can solve. It also moves a sponsor-level decision to the board unnecessarily.

options.text: Hold the decision until the next board meeting in five weeks, when the extension can be approved formally with all the members present.
options.rationale: Waiting five weeks puts the migration supplier's continuity at risk when the sponsor can approve the extension now. It treats the board as the only route when the authority already sits with an available individual.

options.text: Send her a one-page decision note with your recommendation for her explicit approval, and offer to draft a recorded delegation if she wants a higher limit.
options.rationale: It makes approval as easy as possible for a sponsor who trusts you, while keeping the decision with the person who holds the authority. If she wants to delegate more, the governance plan already provides a recorded way to do it.

questions.explanation: Trust from a sponsor does not change who holds an authority; only a delegation made the way the governance arrangements require does that. When a decision-maker is happy to defer to you, the right response is to make their decision effortless and, if appropriate, to formalise a defined delegation, rather than act on an informal blessing with no limits attached.
questions.mindset: Make it easy for the owner to decide, rather than deciding for them because they let you.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme at a regional airport, the board has failed at three consecutive meetings to choose between two baggage-handling systems, splitting three votes to three each time. The terms of reference give the sponsor, as chair, a casting vote, but she has held back in the hope of consensus. Two software teams are now filling sprints with low-value work, and the preferred supplier's price expires in five weeks. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Commission an independent study of a third option, so that the board has fresh evidence that may break the three-to-three split.
options.rationale: A third study adds time and a third contender for a body that cannot choose between two. Fresh evidence does not resolve a split that is about preference rather than missing facts.

options.text: Put the monthly cost of delay, including the teams' low-value work and the price expiry, in front of the board alongside the decision paper.
options.rationale: Boards defer when delay looks free. Showing the cost of each month of indecision makes waiting a choice with a price, which is often what moves a split body to decide.

options.text: Have the software teams build interfaces for both systems, so that the delay costs less whichever option the board finally chooses.
options.rationale: Building for both spends delivery capacity hedging a decision the governance can already make, and it reduces the pressure on the board to make it. It is a costly way of avoiding the real issue.

options.text: Escalate the choice to the airport's executive committee, since the board has shown three times that it cannot reach a decision.
options.rationale: The board has a decision rule it has not yet used, so it has not reached the limit of its authority. Escalating past a level that can still decide undermines that level and spends executive time.

options.text: Before the next meeting, ask the chair whether she will use the casting vote the terms of reference give her if the board splits again.
options.rationale: The terms of reference already contain the mechanism for breaking a tie. Raising it privately with the chair respects her position while making clear that the governance has an answer she can use.

questions.explanation: A deadlocked governance body usually needs two things: a clear view of what indecision is costing, and a reminder of the decision rule its own terms provide. Escalation and further analysis are for when the body has exhausted its authority or genuinely lacks information, not for when it has the means to decide and is reluctant to use them.
questions.mindset: Make the cost of not deciding visible, and point to the rule that lets someone decide.

questions.stem: Both judgements arise on a hybrid programme replacing an ambulance service's call-triage system. Complete each sentence with the role whose view the board should rely on. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: At the stage review, the board must judge whether the new triage screens will work for call handlers during a busy night shift. The board should rely on the view of
The board must judge whether the supplier's plan for the next three increments is technically achievable with the engineers the supplier has committed. The board should rely on the view of

options.text: the senior user, who represents the people who will use the outputs
options.rationale: Fitness for use is judged by those who will live with the result. The senior user speaks for the call handlers and is accountable for confirming that what is delivered meets their needs.

options.text: the senior supplier, who represents those providing the expertise and resources
options.rationale: Technical feasibility and the adequacy of committed resources are the senior supplier's to vouch for, because that role is accountable for what the suppliers can deliver.

options.text: the sponsor, who owns the business case and overall value for money
options.rationale: Not used. The sponsor decides whether the investment is still worth making, drawing on both views, but is not the source of either judgement. The candidate picks the most senior member rather than the one accountable for the specific question.

options.text: project assurance, which checks independently on the board's behalf
options.rationale: Not used. Assurance checks that the board's information is sound; it does not replace the judgement of the member accountable for the area. The candidate confuses verifying a view with providing it.

questions.explanation: A project board is designed so that business, user and supplier interests are each represented by a member accountable for them. When the board needs a judgement, it should come from the member whose interest the question belongs to, with assurance verifying it independently and the sponsor weighing the views together. Asking the most senior or the most independent person instead loses the accountability the structure was built to provide.
questions.mindset: Route each judgement to the member accountable for that interest, not to whoever is most senior.
